tagline: Own the servers everything runs on — patching, backups, identity, and the maintenance windows nobody sees.
what_you_do: You keep a company's servers, identities, and core services alive: patching operating systems, managing Active Directory and Entra ID accounts, running virtualization hosts, watching monitoring dashboards, and making sure last night's backups actually worked. It's the generalist infrastructure role — when something between the desktop and the network breaks, it lands on you. Almost nobody starts here day one; the normal route is a year or two in help desk or a NOC, picking up server tasks until they become your job. Be clear-eyed about the trajectory too: the classic on-prem version of this role is shrinking as workloads move to the cloud, so the modern sysadmin path deliberately ends in hybrid and cloud administration.
day_in_life: Check monitoring and backup reports first thing — rerun the one backup job that failed and find out why
Work the escalations support couldn't crack: a service that won't start, a full disk, a Group Policy doing something weird
Stage this month's patches on test servers ahead of Saturday night's maintenance window
Provision accounts, group memberships, and mailboxes in Active Directory/Entra for Monday's new hires
Turn a manual task into a PowerShell script and schedule it so nobody ever does it by hand again

salary.entry: ~$60,000 to start (junior roles, usually reached from support)
salary.growth: -4% projected — cloud is absorbing the classic on-prem role
salary.note: U.S. BLS figure for Network and Computer Systems Administrators (15-1244); a median is the midpoint of everyone employed, so entry pay runs well below it. The negative outlook is real — it's why this roadmap ends in cloud, not on-prem. Verify against the live BLS page before deciding.

downsides: Patching happens when users are offline, so nights and weekends are part of the deal, and on-call pages come with the pager. The work is invisible when done well — nobody notices the servers until they break, and then everybody does. And the occupation itself is projected to shrink as cloud absorbs on-prem work: staying valuable means continuously retooling toward cloud and automation, not settling in.

fits_if: You like being the person who understands how the whole environment fits together
You get satisfaction from quiet reliability — systems that just work
You'd rather spend an hour automating a task than repeat it forever
less_ideal_if: You need visible wins — good sysadmin work goes unnoticed by design
You want strictly 9-to-5 with no maintenance windows or on-call
You're hoping to learn one stack once and coast — this role is mid-transition to cloud

skills.name: Operating systems (Windows Server + Linux)
skills.note: Most shops run both — being fluent in only one halves your options.

skills.name: Networking fundamentals
skills.note: Servers are network citizens; you can't troubleshoot one without understanding the other.

skills.name: Identity & directory services (Active Directory / Entra ID)
Backup & recovery
skills.note: The unglamorous discipline that actually ends careers when it's neglected.

skills.name: Scripting & automation (PowerShell / Bash)
skills.note: The single biggest lever for pay, promotion, and surviving the cloud shift.

skills.name: Cloud administration (Azure / Microsoft 365)
skills.note: Where the role is going — hybrid identity and cloud workloads.

certs.title: CompTIA Network+
certs.reason: Servers live on networks — this is the assumed baseline.

certs.title: CompTIA Linux+
certs.reason: Linux administration fundamentals — half the server world runs on it.

certs.title: Microsoft AZ-104 (Administrator)
certs.reason: The associate cert proving you can operate the hybrid/cloud infrastructure sysadmin work is becoming.

certs.title: Google IT Automation with Python
certs.reason: Python, Git, and config management — the scripting skills that separate 'keeps it running' from 'automated it away.'

cert_note: If you land in a Linux-heavy shop, Red Hat's hands-on RHCSA is the respected next step (no guide here yet). Either way, a home lab you can talk through in an interview outweighs any certificate on this list.

trial.objective: Do the core sysadmin move: find a task you repeat on your own computer, automate it with a script, and schedule it to run itself.
trial.disclosure: Built-in tools only — PowerShell + Task Scheduler on Windows, Bash + cron on Mac/Linux. Nothing installed, everything stays on your machine.

roadmap.title: Learn the fundamentals
roadmap.focus: TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP — servers are network citizens first. Free via Professor Messer; spin up a home lab with VirtualBox or a spare PC.

roadmap.title: Get fluent in operating systems
roadmap.focus: Learn Linux administration properly (users, permissions, services, storage) and lab Windows Server alongside it — free evaluation ISOs exist for exactly this.

roadmap.title: Start on the support rung and automate
roadmap.focus: Take the help desk / NOC / junior admin job — that's the honest door in. Volunteer for every server task, and script anything you do twice. Automation is what gets you promoted out.

roadmap.title: Go hybrid and cloud
roadmap.focus: Extend what you know upward: Active Directory to Entra ID, on-prem VMs to Azure. AZ-104 proves you can run the environment this job is turning into.

roadmap.title: Pick your exit ramp
roadmap.focus: Classic on-prem administration is a shrinking island. Ride your foundation toward a growing shore: cloud/platform engineering (infrastructure as code) or security.

adjacent_paths.reason: The natural evolution of the role as infrastructure moves to code and cloud.
Deeply overlapping infrastructure disciplines that feed each other.
